opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think it's worth separating two questions. One is the historical question: how much of AI progress so far has come from better software, meaning algorithms, architectures, training recipes, data, versus simply scaling up the compute we throw at these systems. The other is the forward-looking question of whether software could take over as the main driver, especially once AI systems can do AI research themselves.

On the historical side, our work suggests both have mattered a lot. When you look at something like language modeling, the compute needed to reach a given level of performance has been falling quite quickly, roughly halving every year or less. That's substantial. But physical compute used in frontier training runs has been growing even faster, something like four to five times per year. So if you decompose the gains, scaling compute has probably been the larger contributor, with algorithmic progress a significant but secondary share. And many algorithmic improvements seem to pay off more at larger scales, so the two aren't really independent. A lot of software progress is itself enabled by having more compute to experiment with.

That's what makes me somewhat skeptical of the strongest versions of the "software takes over" story, the idea that once you automate AI researchers you get a rapid, self-reinforcing software-only intelligence explosion. The crux is how much software progress depends on compute for running experiments. If researchers need to run lots of training runs to find and validate better algorithms, then even with vastly more research labor, you hit a bottleneck: you can't just think your way to better algorithms without testing them. Labor and compute look like complements in that process, not substitutes. Doubling the number of researchers without more experimental compute probably gives you much less than double the progress.

That said, I don't think you can rule it out. There are real uncertainties. We don't have great estimates of the returns to research effort in software, and it's possible that AI researchers would be dramatically more efficient than humans: running smaller-scale experiments that extrapolate well, making fewer mistakes, working in parallel. If the returns to cognitive effort are high enough, you could see software progress accelerate meaningfully, at least for a while, before running into diminishing returns or hardware limits.

So my overall view is that software becoming dominant is plausible during some phase, particularly around the time AI meaningfully automates R&D, but I'd expect compute and hardware scaling, and the broader economic investment that drives them, to remain central. The most likely picture is that both accelerate together, rather than software running off on its own while compute stays fixed.

r001.rationale: The response compares annual rates of compute growth and efficiency improvement, but does not state that software advances can occur on shorter timescales than hardware scaling.

r002.rationale: It says software progress could accelerate when AI meaningfully automates R&D and could become dominant during some phase.

r003.rationale: It explains that finding and validating better algorithms requires experimental compute, and that adding researchers without more compute yields less progress.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we've thought about quite a bit at Epoch. The way I'd frame it is that there are really three main inputs driving AI progress right now: compute, data, and algorithms, or software broadly construed. And the question is whether that third one, software, could become self-reinforcing in a way that decouples progress from the physical constraints on the other two.

Historically, our best estimates suggest that algorithmic progress has been contributing something on the order of half of the effective compute gains we've seen in language models. So roughly, every eight months or so you get a halving of the compute needed to reach a given level of performance, purely from better algorithms, better architectures, better training recipes. That's already a very large contribution. It's comparable to the contribution from just scaling up hardware budgets.

Now, the scenario people worry about, or get excited about depending on your disposition, is one where AI systems themselves start doing a meaningful share of the research that produces those algorithmic improvements. If you have models that can substantially automate the work of AI researchers, then the returns to software R&D could compound. You improve the models, the improved models do better research, which improves the models further. And the key thing is that this loop runs on software, which can be iterated on much faster than building fabs or securing power contracts.

Whether this actually results in a software-driven explosion depends on a few empirical questions. One is the returns to research effort. If you double the amount of cognitive labor going into AI research, how much more algorithmic progress do you get? Our estimates suggest that the returns are fairly high, high enough that if you really could multiply the research workforce by orders of magnitude, you'd see a dramatic acceleration. But there's real uncertainty in those elasticities.

The second question is how much compute bottlenecks the research itself. A lot of AI research isn't just thinking, it's running experiments. And experiments require compute. So even if you had ten thousand automated researchers, they'd be competing for the same GPUs to validate their ideas. That's a brake on the feedback loop. Though I'd note that smarter researchers might be more compute-efficient in their experimentation, choosing better experiments, running smaller-scale proxies, and so on.

The third is just how much low-hanging fruit remains in algorithm space. There might be diminishing returns as you exhaust the easy wins. Although so far we haven't seen strong evidence of that; the rate of algorithmic progress has been fairly steady.

So my overall assessment is that I think it's quite plausible, maybe more likely than not, that software becomes the dominant contributor at some point in the next decade or so, conditional on AI systems becoming capable enough to substantially automate research. I don't think it's guaranteed. The compute bottleneck on experimentation is real and I think somewhat underrated by people who are very bullish on this. But the basic mechanism is sound, and if you look at the trends, we're already in a regime where software matters roughly as much as hardware. It wouldn't take that much for the balance to tip.

r001.rationale: The response says software can be iterated on much faster than building fabs or securing power contracts.

r002.rationale: It explains that AI systems could automate AI research, creating a compounding loop in which better models produce further algorithmic improvements.

r003.rationale: It says research experiments require compute and that even many automated researchers would compete for GPUs to validate their ideas.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s quite plausible, but I’d distinguish two things. One is whether improvements in algorithms and software contribute more to AI progress than increases in hardware. The other is whether software becomes the main constraint on further progress. Those aren’t necessarily the same question.

Software improvements can let you achieve the same capability with less compute, or get more capability from a fixed compute budget. And those improvements can accumulate across the training process: better architectures, better optimization, better use of data. So even if each individual improvement looks modest, their combined effect could be substantial.

What makes this particularly interesting is the possibility that AI systems themselves become useful at doing that research. If they can propose improvements, implement them, and run experiments, then the amount of effort devoted to improving AI software could grow very quickly. That would provide a mechanism by which software advances could become a much larger contributor to progress.

But I wouldn’t regard that as inevitable. Research might become harder, and testing ideas still requires compute and time. Hardware and software are also complementary: more compute makes it possible to discover and exploit better algorithms. So I think software becoming dominant is a serious possibility, especially with increasing automation of research, but I’m less confident that we can cleanly separate its contribution from the contribution of compute.

r001.rationale: The response discusses software and hardware contributions but does not say software advances can happen on shorter timescales than hardware scaling.

r002.rationale: It says AI systems could propose, implement, and test improvements, making effort devoted to software research grow quickly and software a larger contributor to progress.

r003.rationale: It notes that testing ideas requires compute and time, but does not explain that scaling the number of human or AI researchers requires scaling compute to validate their proposed innovations.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that’s quite plausible, although I’d distinguish software becoming the dominant contributor from software becoming the only important contributor. You can still have very substantial growth in compute while improvements in algorithms account for an increasing share of progress.

One reason to expect that is that AI itself could accelerate the process of discovering better algorithms. At the moment, research depends heavily on human researchers trying ideas, running experiments, and interpreting the results. If we can automate more of that process, the amount of effort going into improving AI could grow much faster than the human research workforce.

But there are a couple of uncertainties. One is whether algorithmic discoveries become harder to find as we make progress. Another is how much experimentation those discoveries require. Software research still consumes compute, so these aren’t entirely separate inputs: having more compute lets you run more experiments, and better algorithms let you get more out of your compute.

So I would take the possibility seriously, especially if AI becomes very useful at doing AI research. But I’m less confident about when that happens, or whether we’ll be able to cleanly attribute the resulting progress to software rather than to the combination of software and hardware.

r001.rationale: The response discusses growth in compute and algorithmic progress, but does not compare their timescales or say software advances can happen faster than hardware scaling.

r002.rationale: It says automating AI research could make effort on improving AI grow much faster than the human research workforce, while algorithmic improvements account for an increasing share of progress.

r003.rationale: The response notes that software research consumes compute and that compute enables more experiments, but does not explain that scaling the number of researchers requires scaling compute to validate their proposed innovations.
